title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about putting reflection to work. You already know what reflection is and why it matters; now you will turn it into a practice you can actually carry out. By the end you will be able to use a structured reflective cycle to work through an experience, reflect critically on it rather than only describing it, and turn that reflection into a concrete action for next time.

Reflection is one of the habits that separates a self-regulating learner from a passive one. Done well, it is how you learn from what you do, not just how much you do. These three moves, structure, depth and action, are what make reflection change your next piece of work rather than sit unused in a notebook.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: use a structured reflective cycle to work through an experience
reflect critically on an experience rather than only describing it
turn a reflection into a concrete action that improves your next attempt.

title: In real academic practice
body: Reflection is built into how academic and professional work improves. Every placement log, every portfolio, every time a tutor asks what you would do differently, draws on the same practice. Learning to reflect with structure, depth and a clear action now means each experience in your studies becomes something you genuinely learn from, and the habit carries directly into professional life.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, reflecting with a structure: using a cycle so you work through an experience in set stages rather than at random. Second, from describing to reflecting: pushing past what happened to why it happened and what it means. Third, turning reflection into action: closing the loop so a reflection produces something you will actually do. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.

title: Orientation
body: You already know that reflection matters. The difficulty is usually in the doing: left to itself, reflection tends to wander, or stop at 'that went badly'. A reflective cycle fixes this by giving reflection a shape, a set of stages to work through in turn, so that thinking about an experience leads somewhere. This lesson introduces one such cycle and puts it to work.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are not only recognising that reflection is useful; you are expected to carry it out with a structure and apply it to your own experiences. The aim of this lesson is for you to take a recent experience and work it through a cycle yourself, rather than reflect at random.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain that structured reflection means working through an experience in set stages, rather than at random
recognise the stages of a reflective cycle at work in a worked example
apply a reflective cycle to a recent experience in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Structured reflection means working through an experience in set stages rather than letting your thoughts drift. A reflective cycle names those stages and puts them in order. A simple and widely used one is the ERA cycle: Experience, Reflect, Act. You start from a concrete experience, you reflect on it by asking what happened and why it matters, and you decide on an action to take forward.

The value of a cycle is that it stops reflection stalling. Without a structure, it is easy to describe an experience and go no further, or to jump straight to a vague resolution to do better. Working through set stages makes sure you move from the experience, through genuine reflection, to something you will actually do.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a recent experience in your studies that did not go as you hoped. Walk it through the cycle for yourself: what happened, why, and what one thing you will do differently next time?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Structured reflection means working through an experience in set stages rather than at random, and a cycle such as Experience, Reflect, Act gives you those stages. You can now explain why a structure matters, recognise the stages at work in an example, and apply the cycle to one of your own experiences. The next lesson works on the stage that does the most work: reflecting, rather than only describing.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson the cycle had a stage called Reflect, and it is the stage that does the real work. It is also the one most people skip: it is easy to describe what happened and think you have reflected. This lesson is about the difference between describing an experience and reflecting on it, and how to push a surface reflection deeper.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to do more than notice that reflection should go beyond description. The aim here is for you to take a thin, descriptive reflection and deepen it yourself, asking the questions that turn an account of what happened into an understanding of why.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain the difference between describing what happened and reflecting critically on it
tell description apart from reflection in a worked example
deepen a surface reflection on an experience in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Description answers the question 'what happened?'. It gives an accurate account of the experience: what you did, what others did, how it turned out. Reflection goes further and asks 'so what?' and 'why?'. It looks for the reasons behind what happened, what it tells you about your own approach, and what it means for what you do next. Description is necessary, but on its own it does not change anything.

The move from describing to reflecting is what the evaluation stage of self-regulated learning calls looking back critically: examining your own actions and decisions, honestly, to understand them better. A reflection that only reports events, however carefully, has not yet done this. The questions 'why did that happen?' and 'what does it tell me?' are what turn a description into a reflection.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Take a recent experience in your studies that you could describe easily. Now push past the description: why did it happen the way it did, and what did your own approach have to do with it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Description answers 'what happened'; reflection answers 'so what' and 'why', looking back critically at your own actions and decisions. You can now explain the difference, tell one from the other in an example, and deepen a thin reflection by asking why something happened and what your part in it was. The next lesson takes the understanding you reach and turns it into action.

title: Orientation
body: A reflection that reaches a clear understanding but changes nothing has stopped one step short. The point of reflecting is to do something different next time. This lesson is about closing the loop: turning what you have understood into a concrete action, and seeing how a fuller model of learning from experience builds the action in from the start.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are expected to produce the action yourself, not just agree that action matters. The aim here is for you to take a reflection and turn it into something concrete and usable, an action specific enough that you could carry it out, and that would genuinely change the next attempt.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain that a reflective cycle is complete only when it produces a concrete action for next time
tell a concrete, usable action apart from a vague intention in a worked example
produce a concrete action from a reflection on an experience in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Reflection earns its place when it changes what you do. A reflective cycle is only complete when it produces an action: something concrete you will do differently, drawn from what you understood. A vague intention, such as try harder or be more organised, is not an action, because there is nothing specific to carry out. A concrete action names what you will do, and ideally when.

Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle sets this out as a fuller model of learning from experience. It describes four modes: having a concrete experience, observing and reflecting on it, forming a general idea or lesson from it (abstract conceptualisation), and then actively trying that idea out (active experimentation). The point to take from it is that the cycle treats the experience as the source of learning only when you move on to test what you have learned in practice. The modes are a way of understanding how learning from experience works, not a rigid order you must follow in lockstep.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Take a reflection you have already reached about your studies, where you understand what went wrong but have not acted on it. What is one concrete action, specific enough to carry out, that would follow from it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A reflective cycle is complete only when it produces a concrete action: something specific you will do differently, not a vague intention to improve. Kolb's cycle shows why, treating experience as the source of learning only when you test what you have learned in practice. You can now explain this, tell a concrete action from a vague one, and produce an action of your own. With structure, depth and action in place, your reflection can change what you do, not just what you think.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Reflection is no longer just something you know you should do: it is a practice you can carry out. You can use a structured cycle to work through an experience in set stages, rather than reflecting at random. You can push past describing what happened to reflecting critically on why it happened and what your part was. And you can turn that reflection into a concrete action that changes your next attempt. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, reflection is something you practise across your degree and beyond. Every placement, portfolio, group project and piece of feedback is a chance to run the cycle: work through the experience, reflect on it with real depth, and act on what you find. It is also what professional life expects, and learning to reflect deliberately now is what the advanced tier of this pathway develops into a full professional practice.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced reflective practice course takes these habits into reflection as a professional practice, sustained, evidenced, and part of how you develop as a graduate. Going wider: the same cycle underpins Work-Based and Experiential Learning, Presenting, and Understanding Learning, Assessment and Feedback, where you put structured reflection to work on real tasks.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The stages of a reflective cycle
body: Four cards on how a reflective cycle works. Turn each to see what the stage asks of you.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over. Work through all four.

back.body: Start from something concrete that actually happened: a seminar you led, an essay that came back marked, a lab session that did not go to plan. Name the experience specifically, rather than reflecting on your studies in general. A clear starting point is what the rest of the cycle works on.

Look back at the experience and ask what happened and why. What went well, what did not, and what might explain it? This is where you move past 'it was fine' or 'it went badly' to reasons. It is the heart of the cycle, and the next lesson works on it in depth.

Decide what you will do differently next time. The action should be concrete enough to carry out: not 'prepare better' but 'spend the first hour mapping the question before I read'. Without this stage a reflection stays a thought; with it, the experience changes what you do next.

The stages connect: the action you take becomes the next experience you reflect on, so reflection keeps feeding back into your work. Working in a set order is what stops reflection stalling at description or jumping to a vague resolution.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students are asked to write a short reflection after the same group presentation.

{{learner-a}} writes that the presentation was stressful and the group ran over time, and resolves to be better prepared next time. This touches an experience, but it does not work through it: there is no real reflection on why it ran over, and the action, be better prepared, is too vague to act on. {{learner-a}} has stopped at the experience and jumped to a resolution.

{{learner-b}} starts from the same experience, then reflects: the group ran over because no one had agreed timings, and the nerves came from not having rehearsed the handovers. From that, {{learner-b}} settles on a concrete action, to propose a timed run-through at the next group meeting and agree who speaks when. Experience, reflect, act: each stage done in turn.

Both wrote a reflection. Only {{learner-b}} worked through the cycle, so only {{learner-b}} came away with something usable.

title: Working through the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These habits turn a reflective cycle into something you do. Try them on a recent experience.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I named a specific experience to start from, rather than my studies in general?
Have I said what actually happened, before moving on?
Have I asked why it happened the way it did, not just whether it went well?
Have I reached an action, rather than stopping at the reflection?
Is my action concrete enough that I could carry it out this week?
Have I noticed how this action will shape the next experience I reflect on?

title: Formative check: reflecting with a structure
displayTitle: What does it mean to reflect with a structure, rather than at random?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to reflect with a structure rather than at random?

_items.text: To work through an experience in set stages, from the experience, through reflection, to an action.
_items.feedback: Yes. A cycle moves you through set stages so reflection leads somewhere.

_items.text: To write down as much as possible about how the experience felt.
_items.feedback: Writing a lot is not the same as working through stages; structure is about moving from experience to action.

_items.text: To decide straight away what you will do differently next time.
_items.feedback: Jumping to an action skips the reflection stage; a cycle works through each stage in turn.

_items.text: To judge whether the experience went well or badly.
_items.feedback: A verdict is not reflection; the cycle asks why it went as it did and what to do.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A cycle moves you through set stages, from the experience, through reflection, to an action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about working through set stages, rather than writing a lot or jumping to a resolution.
_incorrect.final: Reflecting with a structure means working through set stages, from the experience, through reflection, to an action. Writing more, resolving at once or judging the outcome are not the same.

title: Formative check: recognising the stages
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's reflection a worked-through cycle rather than a stalled one?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's reflection a worked-through cycle?

_items.text: They reflected on why the presentation ran over, then set a concrete action from it.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reflecting on the reasons and then acting is the cycle worked through.

_items.text: They wrote more about the experience than the first student.
_items.feedback: Length is not the point; working through the stages is.

_items.text: They resolved to be better prepared next time.
_items.feedback: That is the vague resolution the first student stopped at.

_items.text: They found the presentation less stressful.
_items.feedback: How stressful it felt does not show the cycle being worked through.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reflecting on why it happened and then setting a concrete action is the cycle worked through.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the student who reflected on the reasons AND acted on them.
_incorrect.final: The second student worked through the cycle by reflecting on why it ran over and then setting a concrete action. Writing more, resolving vaguely or feeling calmer are not the same.

title: Formative check: applying the cycle
displayTitle: You are reflecting on a recent experience in {{context}}. Which approach applies the cycle this lesson describes?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach applies the reflective cycle to a recent experience?

_items.text: Name what happened, work out why it happened, then decide one concrete thing to do next time.
_items.feedback: Yes. Experience, reflect, act is the cycle applied to your work in {{context}}.

_items.text: Write down how the experience made you feel and leave it there.
_items.feedback: Recording a feeling is not working through the cycle to an action.

_items.text: Decide immediately to work harder on the next one.
_items.feedback: That jumps to a vague resolution and skips the reflection stage.

_items.text: Judge whether it went well and move on.
_items.feedback: A verdict is not the cycle; it asks why, and what you will do.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, applying the cycle means moving from the experience, through why it happened, to a concrete action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that moves from the experience, through why, to a concrete action.
_incorrect.final: Applying the cycle in {{context}} means naming what happened, working out why, and deciding a concrete action. Recording a feeling, resolving to work harder or judging the outcome all stop short.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Four moves from description to reflection
body: Four moves that turn an account of what happened into a reflection. Open each to see the move.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: From what to why
_items.body: A description says what happened. Reflection asks why it happened that way. Moving from the event to its causes is the first step out of pure description: instead of 'the seminar was quiet', you ask what made it quiet and what part you played.

_items.title: From the event to yourself
_items.body: Critical reflection turns some of the attention back on you: what did your own choices, assumptions or preparation contribute? This is not about blame; it is about seeing your part clearly enough to change it.

_items.title: From judgement to evidence
_items.body: 'It went badly' is a verdict, not a reflection. Deepening it means pointing to what actually happened that led you to that verdict, the specific moment, comment or result, so your reflection rests on evidence rather than a feeling.

_items.title: From then to next time
_items.body: A reflection earns its place when it points forward. Asking 'what does this tell me for next time?' connects the understanding you have reached to what you will do, and leads into the action the next lesson is about.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students write a reflection on the same piece of coursework that came back with a lower mark than they expected.

{{learner-a}} writes that the essay lost marks on structure and that the feedback said the argument was hard to follow. This is accurate, and it is entirely description: it reports what happened and what the feedback said, but it does not ask why the structure was weak or what {{learner-a}} did that led to it. The account stops at what happened.

{{learner-b}} starts from the same facts, then reflects: the argument was hard to follow because {{learner-b}} started writing before deciding on a line of argument, so each paragraph set off in its own direction. The low mark was not bad luck but a consequence of planning too little. That is a reflection: it reaches a reason, and it points to {{learner-b}}'s own approach.

Both described the same experience accurately. Only {{learner-b}} reflected on it, by asking why it happened and what their own part was.

title: Deepening a reflection
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These questions turn a description into a reflection. Try them on something you could already describe.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I said what happened, before trying to explain it?
Have I asked why it happened that way, not just whether it went well?
Have I looked at what my own choices or preparation contributed?
Have I backed any verdict with something specific that happened?
Have I asked what this tells me for next time?
Would someone reading this learn why, not just what?

title: Formative check: description versus reflection
displayTitle: What is the difference between describing an experience and reflecting on it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the difference between describing an experience and reflecting on it?

_items.text: Description says what happened; reflection asks why it happened and what it means.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reflection goes beyond the account to reasons and meaning.

_items.text: Description is short; reflection is long.
_items.feedback: Length is not the difference; a long account can still be pure description.

_items.text: Description is about other people; reflection is about facts.
_items.feedback: Both can involve you and others; the difference is 'what' versus 'why'.

_items.text: Description is for seminars; reflection is for essays.
_items.feedback: The difference is not where you do it, but whether you reach the reasons.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Description reports what happened; reflection asks why, and what it means.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The difference is between reporting what happened and reaching why it happened.
_incorrect.final: Description says what happened; reflection asks why and what it means. Length, subject and setting are not the difference.

title: Formative check: telling them apart
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's account a reflection rather than a description?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's account a reflection rather than a description?

_items.text: They reached a reason for the low mark and pointed to their own planning.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reaching a reason and looking at their own part is reflection.

_items.text: They reported the feedback more accurately.
_items.feedback: Accurate reporting is still description.

_items.text: They wrote at greater length about the essay.
_items.feedback: Length does not turn a description into a reflection.

_items.text: They felt more strongly about the mark.
_items.feedback: A stronger feeling is not a reflection on why it happened.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reaching a reason for the mark, and pointing to their own planning, is what makes it a reflection.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student worked out, beyond reporting the feedback.
_incorrect.final: The second student reflected by reaching a reason for the low mark and pointing to their own planning. Accurate reporting, extra length or a stronger feeling are all still description.

title: Formative check: deepening a reflection
displayTitle: Your reflection on an experience in {{context}} so far only reports what happened. Which move deepens it into a critical reflection?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which move deepens a descriptive account into a reflection?

_items.text: Ask why it happened that way and what your own approach contributed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Asking why, and looking at your own part, turns a description of {{context}} work into a reflection.

_items.text: Add more detail about what happened.
_items.feedback: More detail is still description, however thorough.

_items.text: State more firmly whether it went well or badly.
_items.feedback: A firmer verdict is not a reason; it is still not reflection.

_items.text: Describe how it made you feel.
_items.feedback: A record of the feeling does not reach why it happened.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, asking why and examining your own part is what deepens a description into a reflection.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that reaches why it happened, rather than adding detail or a verdict.
_incorrect.final: Deepening a reflection on {{context}} work means asking why it happened and what your approach contributed. More detail, a firmer verdict or a note of feeling all stay at description.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The four modes of Kolb's cycle
body: Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle describes four modes of learning from experience. Select each tab to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each tab to read about that mode.

_items.title: Concrete experience
_items.body: You do something, or something happens to you: a placement shift, a seminar, a piece of assessed work. This is the raw material the rest of the cycle works on. Learning starts from real experience, not from theory alone.

_items.title: Reflective observation
_items.body: You look back on the experience and notice what happened and how, from more than one angle. This is the reflecting stage: watching the experience again in your mind and asking what stands out.

_items.title: Abstract conceptualisation
_items.body: You form a general lesson from the experience: not just 'that meeting went badly' but 'meetings without an agreed agenda tend to drift'. Turning one experience into a transferable idea is what lets it shape more than the next identical situation.

_items.title: Active experimentation
_items.body: You try the lesson out in practice: you set an agenda for the next meeting and see what happens. This is where reflection becomes action, and the result becomes the next concrete experience. Without this step the cycle never closes.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students have each reflected well on why a lab report lost marks, and reach the same understanding: they wrote up the method from memory, days later, and left gaps. Now each decides what to do about it.

{{learner-a}} resolves to take the write-up more seriously next time and to be more careful with the method. This is a genuine intention, but it is not an action: there is nothing specific to carry out, and 'more careful' could mean anything. Next time will probably look much like last time.

{{learner-b}} decides to write the method section during the session itself, filling a template at each step before leaving the lab. That is a concrete action: it names what to do and when, it follows directly from the reflection, and it would genuinely change the next report. The loop is closed.

Both understood the problem equally well. Only {{learner-b}} turned that understanding into something that will actually change the next attempt.

title: Turning reflection into action
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: These questions check that a reflection has produced a concrete action. Try them on a reflection of your own.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Does my action follow directly from what I reflected on?
Have I named what I will do, specifically, rather than how I will be?
Could someone else tell whether I had done it?
Have I said when or where I will do it?
Is it something I could actually carry out before the next attempt?
Will doing it genuinely change the next experience, not just my intentions?

title: Formative check: when the cycle is complete
displayTitle: When is a reflective cycle complete?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: When is a reflective cycle complete?

_items.text: When it produces a concrete action you will take next time.
_items.feedback: Yes. The cycle closes when understanding turns into a concrete action.

_items.text: When you have understood why the experience happened.
_items.feedback: Understanding is the reflection stage; the cycle closes only when it leads to an action.

_items.text: When you have described the experience in full.
_items.feedback: A full description is only the start of the cycle.

_items.text: When you have decided whether it went well or badly.
_items.feedback: A verdict is not an action; the cycle needs something you will do.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A reflective cycle is complete only when it produces a concrete action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Understanding and description come earlier; what closes the cycle?
_incorrect.final: A reflective cycle is complete only when it produces a concrete action for next time. Understanding, describing or judging the experience all stop short of that.

title: Formative check: concrete action or vague intention
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's response a concrete action rather than a vague intention?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's response a concrete action?

_items.text: It named exactly what to do and when: write the method during the session, on a template.
_items.feedback: Yes. Naming what to do, and when, makes it a concrete action.

_items.text: It took the problem more seriously.
_items.feedback: Taking it seriously is an attitude, not an action.

_items.text: It showed more understanding of why marks were lost.
_items.feedback: Both students understood equally well; the difference was the action.

_items.text: It was a stronger resolution to be careful.
_items.feedback: 'Be careful' is the vague intention, not a concrete action.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Naming exactly what to do, and when, is what makes it a concrete action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the response that names exactly what to do and when.
_incorrect.final: The second student's response was a concrete action because it named what to do and when. Taking the problem seriously, understanding it or resolving to be careful are not actions.

title: Formative check: producing an action
displayTitle: You have reflected on an experience in {{context}} and understood what went wrong. Which is a concrete action rather than a vague intention?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is a concrete action rather than a vague intention?

_items.text: A specific step you will take next time, named clearly enough to carry out and check.
_items.feedback: Yes. A concrete action in {{context}} names what you will do, so you could actually carry it out.

_items.text: A resolution to approach the work more seriously.
_items.feedback: That is an attitude, not something specific to carry out.

_items.text: A decision to try harder next time.
_items.feedback: 'Try harder' names nothing specific to do.

_items.text: A clearer sense of why it went wrong.
_items.feedback: That is still understanding; the cycle needs an action.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A concrete action in {{context}} names a specific step you could carry out and check.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that names a specific step, rather than an attitude or more understanding.
_incorrect.final: A concrete action in {{context}} is a specific step, named clearly enough to carry out and check. Resolving to be serious, to try harder, or understanding more are not actions.

body: What does it mean to reflect with a structure rather than at random?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to reflect with a structure rather than at random?

_items.text: To work through an experience in set stages, from the experience, through reflection, to an action.
To write down everything you can remember about the experience.
To decide at once what you will do differently.
To judge whether the experience went well or badly.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reflecting with a structure means working through set stages to an action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about working through set stages, from experience to action.

body: A reflective cycle such as Experience, Reflect, Act is most useful because it...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is a reflective cycle such as Experience, Reflect, Act most useful?

_items.text: moves you from the experience, through reflection, to a concrete action.
makes you write more about each experience.
tells you whether the experience was a success.
replaces the need to plan your work.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A cycle moves you from experience, through reflection, to a concrete action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What does a cycle move you through, from start to finish?

body: Which of these is a reflection on an experience, rather than only a description of it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these is a reflection rather than only a description?

_items.text: The seminar was quiet because I had not prepared questions, so discussion had nothing to start from.
The seminar was quiet and lasted an hour.
The seminar covered three readings and two students spoke.
The seminar did not go well.

_feedback.correct: That's right. It reaches a reason and points to the student's own part, which is reflection.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that reaches a reason, not just an account or a verdict.

body: A student writes a careful, accurate account of what happened on a placement, but asks no questions about why. What is missing?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A careful account that asks no questions about why is missing what?

_items.text: The reflection: there is description, but no 'why' or 'so what'.
Nothing; a full account is a complete reflection.
More detail about what happened.
A clearer verdict on how it went.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The account describes but does not reflect: there is no 'why' or 'so what'.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A careful account can still be pure description; what has not been done?

body: Which of these is a concrete action drawn from a reflection, rather than a vague intention?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which of these is a concrete action rather than a vague intention?

_items.text: Map the essay question and agree a line of argument before writing the first paragraph.
Be more organised with my essays from now on.
Take my coursework more seriously.
Try to plan better next time.

_feedback.correct: That's right. It names a specific step you could carry out, which is a concrete action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that names a specific step, not an attitude.

body: According to Kolb's Experiential Learning Cycle, an experience becomes a source of learning only when you...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: In Kolb's cycle, an experience becomes a source of learning only when you do what?

_items.text: test what you have learned from it in practice.
describe it in as much detail as possible.
decide whether it went well.
remember it for the next exam.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The cycle treats experience as a source of learning only when you test what you learned in practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Kolb's cycle closes when you try the lesson out; which option says that?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: working through an experience with a structure, reflecting critically rather than only describing, and turning a reflection into a concrete action. On their own they are three separate moves. This lesson brings them together into one practice.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to run a perfect reflection every time. The aim is to see these three moves as one practice rather than three separate ideas, so reflection becomes something you carry out across the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect a structured cycle, critical reflection and a concrete action as one reflective practice
analyse how a structured cycle, critical reflection and a concrete action work as one in a worked example
apply the whole reflective practice to an experience in your {{context}} study this term

title: Concept: definition
body: Reflective practice is these three moves working as one, not three separate tasks. Each time you reflect, you run a structured cycle, you push past describing to a real reason, and you finish with a concrete action. The three moves from the earlier lessons are the parts of that one practice.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, you do not run these three moves on separate occasions. On one piece of work you look back with a structure, reach an honest reason, and set a concrete action, all in the same sitting. Run that way, each experience in your studies becomes something you genuinely learn from.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of work you have coming up. How will you run the whole practice on it: a structured look back, an honest reason, and one concrete action? When will you start?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Reflection is most useful when the three moves work as one practice. On any experience you look back with a structure, reach an honest reason, and set a concrete action to carry forward. It is running the whole practice, again and again across your studies, that changes how you work.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: The three moves work as one continuing cycle, not three separate tasks. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Describe
_items.body: Start from the experience and set out clearly what happened, before you move on to judging or explaining it.

_items.title: Ask why
_items.body: Reflect critically - ask why it happened and what your own part in it was, pushing past the description to a real reason.

_items.title: Decide an action
_items.body: Decide one concrete action, specific enough to carry out next time rather than a vague intention to do better.

_items.title: Carry forward
_items.body: Carry that action into your next attempt, then look back again and run the cycle once more. The practice keeps turning.

_diagram.title: Reflective practice as a continuing cycle

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students reflect across a whole module. One treats each task fresh: a quick note here, a vague resolution there, with the structure, the reason and the action never joined up. The other runs the whole practice each time, looking back with a structure, reaching a real reason, and setting one concrete action to carry forward. Over the module, the second student's work improves, because reflection had become one practice rather than three odd jobs.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to run the whole practice
body: Use these to check you have run the whole practice, not just one part of it.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I start from the experience and set out what actually happened?
Did I reflect on why it happened, not just describe it?
Did I look honestly at my own part in it?
Did I end with one concrete action, specific enough to carry out?
Did I carry that action into my next piece of work?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat these three moves as one practice rather than three separate ideas?
body: Why is it more useful to treat these three moves as one practice rather than three separate ideas?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat these three moves as one practice rather than three separate ideas?

_items.text: Because they only pay off together: a structured cycle gives reflection shape, depth finds the real reason, and an action makes it change something.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three moves strengthen one another when you run them together.

_items.text: Because running one move at a time is always quicker than running all three.
_items.feedback: Speed is not the point. The moves are worth most used together.

_items.text: Because only one of the three moves actually matters in the end.
_items.feedback: All three matter. The gain comes from using them together.

_items.text: Because keeping them separate means you never have to settle on an action.
_items.feedback: Ending in an action is one of the moves, not something to avoid.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Structure, depth and action are three parts of one practice, each needing the others.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you gain by running the three moves together on one experience.

displayTitle: A student sets out what happened on a presentation, works out why it overran and what their own part was, and plans one timed run-through for next time. What does this show?
body: A student sets out what happened on a presentation, works out why it overran and what their own part was, and plans one timed run-through for next time. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student sets out what happened on a presentation, works out why it overran and what their own part was, and plans one timed run-through for next time. What does this show?

_items.text: That the three moves are working together as one practice: a structured look back, a real reason, and a concrete action.
_items.feedback: Yes. Structure, depth and action are all in play on the one experience.

_items.text: That the student used only one of the three moves and skipped the rest.
_items.feedback: Look again: the structure, the reason and the action are all there.

_items.text: That reflecting critically cannot be joined to setting an action.
_items.feedback: The example joins them: the reason leads straight to the action.

_items.text: That reflection belongs only after a presentation has gone wrong.
_items.feedback: The practice fits any experience, not only ones that go wrong.

_feedback.correct: That's right. All three moves are at work together on the one experience.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how many of the three moves the student ran.

displayTitle: You want to run the whole reflective practice on your {{context}} study this term. Which plan does that best?
body: You want to run the whole reflective practice on your {{context}} study this term. Which plan does that best?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to run the whole reflective practice on your your subject study this term. Which plan does that best?

_items.text: After each piece of work, run a structured cycle, reach a real reason, and set one concrete action to carry forward.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs all three moves together, piece after piece.

_items.text: Pick the one move you find easiest and use only that all term.
_items.feedback: Using one move alone misses the gain of running them together.

_items.text: Write one long reflection at the end of term and leave it there.
_items.feedback: One reflection at the end is not a practice you run across the term.

_items.text: Wait until a mark disappoints you before reflecting at all.
_items.feedback: Reflection is something you plan from the start, not only when things go wrong.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Running the three moves together, piece after piece, is reflective practice across your study.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which plan runs all three moves together, again and again?

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: What does it mean to treat reflection as one practice rather than three separate moves?
body: What does it mean to treat reflection as one practice rather than three separate moves?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to treat reflection as one practice rather than three separate moves?

_items.text: You run a structured cycle, reflect critically, and set a concrete action on the same experience, using them together.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three moves work together on one experience.

_items.text: You choose one of the three moves and use only it.
_items.feedback: That keeps the moves separate rather than running them together.

_items.text: You reflect only when a piece of work has gone badly.
_items.feedback: The practice fits any experience, not only ones that go wrong.

_items.text: You stop once you understand the problem, without setting an action.
_items.feedback: Ending in an action is part of the practice, not an optional extra.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

displayTitle: A student sets out what happened in a seminar, works out why it fell flat and what their own part was, and plans one change for the next one. Which best describes this?
